items.statement: A team has kept a practice for years that most members, asked privately, say they dislike. The practice can persist indefinitely, because each member reads the others' compliance as approval.
items.folk_theory: Disapproval kills norms: a practice nobody likes cannot last.
items.explanation: Pluralistic ignorance keeps disliked norms alive. Each person infers that others approve from the fact that others comply, and that compliance is itself driven by the same inference. The norm is a shared misperception, and it dies only when the private disapproval becomes common knowledge, through a credible published measurement or a visible trendsetter; it does not fade because each person knows their own view (Bicchieri, The Grammar of Society, ch 5; ledger C44).

items.statement: People will pay out of their own pocket to punish someone who treated them unfairly, even when they will never meet again.
items.folk_theory: People are payoff maximisers: nobody spends money on revenge against a stranger.
items.explanation: Ultimatum-game rejections are robust across decades and countries. In Western student samples about half of offers below a fifth of the pie are rejected (an approximate background figure), and rejection falls sharply when the same low offer is generated by a computer, so what is punished is the inferred intention (Blount 1995). The lab willingness to punish is [E]; what it says about evolution is a separate question (Camerer, Behavioral Game Theory, ch 2; ledger rules 4 and 25).

items.statement: Humans evolved to punish cheats at personal cost, and that evolved trait is what keeps cooperation stable in real communities.
items.folk_theory: Strong reciprocity is settled science and explains real-world cooperation.
items.explanation: Two claims are bundled here. Willingness to pay to punish unfair intentions in the lab is [E]. The claim that this is an evolved trait, strong reciprocity, is contested (Guala 2012; Binmore 2006) and is [H] in this course. Field evidence from durable commons shows that real-world sanctioning is mostly cheap, graduated and run by participants, so designs should rest on the cheap version (Gintis, evidence section; Ostrom ch 3; ledger X4, rule 4).

items.statement: Because Schelling's checkerboard produces segregation from mild preferences, a city's observed segregation is evidence that residents' preferences, not discrimination, produced it.
items.folk_theory: Schelling proved that preferences, not discrimination, produce segregation.
items.explanation: The checkerboard is a possibility proof. It shows that mild preferences plus interdependence can produce extreme sorting, and that homogeneity is weak evidence of intolerance. It says nothing about the real-world share due to discrimination, prices, lending or law, and Schelling says so. Real tipping does exist in US census tracts at roughly 5 to 20 percent minority share, higher where measured tolerance is higher (Card, Mas and Rothstein 2008), which is evidence for the dynamic, not for the cause (Schelling ch 4; ledger C29, rule 17).

items.statement: Two teams both prefer a shared standard to their separate ones, and each knows the other prefers it too. They can still fail to adopt it, because each fears switching while the other does not.
items.folk_theory: The efficient equilibrium is the rational one, so sensible people find it.
items.explanation: A stag hunt has two equilibria, and which one a population reaches depends on the basin of attraction it starts in, not on how attractive the good outcome is. Under random mixing, best-response updating, large groups and no communication the risk-dominant equilibrium usually has the larger basin and wins; laboratory groups converge to it without communication (Cooper et al.; Van Huyck et al.). Choosing the safe action under uncertainty about the others is defensible, so the failure is structural and so is the fix (Skyrms ch 1; Camerer ch 7; ledger X6, rule 2).

items.statement: Ten minutes of relevant, non-binding talk before a public-goods decision roughly doubles cooperation in the lab.
items.folk_theory: Talk is cheap and therefore empty: only binding commitments change behaviour.
items.explanation: In Dawes, McTavish and Shaklee (1977) relevant discussion raised cooperation from roughly a third to roughly seven in ten (approximate background figures), and communication is the strongest single lever in the Sally 1995 meta-analysis. The promises were unenforceable; talk works by creating the empirical and normative expectations a cooperation norm needs. Expect the effect to decay without sanctions or repetition where defection dominates (Bicchieri ch 4; Gilovich et al. ch 14; ledger rule 12).

items.statement: A costly new practice adopted by a tight-knit sub-team of ten is more likely to survive and spread than the same practice seeded in ten well-connected people scattered across the organisation.
items.folk_theory: Clusters are bad: insular sub-groups hold new practices back.
items.explanation: Clusters cut both ways. A cluster whose density exceeds one minus the adoption threshold blocks a cascade entering from outside, and by the same arithmetic it protects a behaviour adopted inside it. Costly behaviour is a complex contagion needing several adopting neighbours, so a scattered seed leaves each adopter below threshold and reverting, while a clustered seed holds and can spread through wide bridges (Centola 2010, background). The rule is: seed inside dense clusters and build wide bridges out of them (Easley and Kleinberg ch 19; ledger X7, rule 3).

items.statement: The reason weak ties matter is that an acquaintance is a better source of job leads and useful information than a close friend is.
items.folk_theory: Weak ties are about job-hunting: acquaintances beat close friends as sources of jobs and information.
items.explanation: The robust claim is structural: by strong triadic closure a local bridge must be a weak tie, and Onnela et al. (2007) confirmed the pattern in phone-network data. The popular job-search claim rests on a small retrospective sample, and later large-scale work found a mixed picture: most jobs still arrive through weak ties in aggregate, because people have many more of them, but any single strong tie is more valuable at the margin (Gee et al. 2017) and moderately weak ties do best (Rajkumar et al. 2022). Quote the structural claim only, and remember that weak ties carry information, not costly behaviour (Easley and Kleinberg ch 3; ledger C51, rule 33).

items.statement: A team schedules its hardest cooperative decisions for the morning, on the grounds that self-control is a resource that gets used up over the day.
items.folk_theory: Ego depletion: self-control is a muscle that tires.
items.explanation: The registered replication of the ego-depletion effect across 23 labs with N = 2,141 found d = 0.04 with a confidence interval including zero (Hagger et al. 2016, verified), and a later multi-lab effort was similar. The course's replication rule is to build nothing on ego depletion, social priming, power posing, watching eyes, the Stanford Prison Experiment as usually told, groupthink as a syndrome or IAT-based training (Gilovich et al., evidence section; ledger C11, rule 20).

items.statement: In Milgram's obedience studies, most participants went to the maximum shock even when a peer beside them refused to continue.
items.folk_theory: Blind obedience: most people will hurt others when told to, whoever else is in the room.
items.explanation: The baseline behaviour replicates: 70 percent continued past 150 volts in Burger's 2009 partial replication (verified) against roughly 82 percent at the same point in Milgram. But obedience fell sharply with victim proximity, an absent authority or a disobedient peer: with two peers refusing, only about one in ten went to the maximum (background figure). Participants were distressed, and archival work shows engaged followership rather than sadism. The design lesson is exits, peers and legitimacy of refusal, not a verdict on human nature (Gilovich et al. ch 9; ledger C21, rule 22).

items.statement: Two parties expect to keep dealing with each other indefinitely, and each can see what the other did last time. Permanent mutual defection is still an equilibrium of their game.
items.folk_theory: Repetition solves the PD: the shadow of the future guarantees cooperation.
items.explanation: The folk theorem is an existence result. With a long, uncertain and observable future, cooperation becomes one equilibrium among many, including permanent mutual defection. The group must still coordinate on the cooperative equilibrium and detect defection fast enough for retaliation to bite, and under noise it needs forgiving strategies. Repetition permits cooperation; selection is a separate problem (Dixit, Skeath and McAdams ch 10; ledger C27, rule 15).

items.statement: A practice that most members follow and that newcomers copy can fail to be a social norm of the group, if nobody expects disapproval for skipping it.
items.folk_theory: Norm equals majority: the norm is what people do.
items.explanation: What most people do is a descriptive norm, sustained by empirical expectations alone and liable to flip when the visible majority changes. A social norm in Bicchieri's sense is a conditional preference that also needs normative expectations, the belief that others think one ought to comply and may sanction; without them a widely followed practice is not a social norm, and a social norm can exist while widely violated. The four-way taxonomy (descriptive, convention, social, moral) tells you which lever to pull (Bicchieri ch 1; ledger C42, rule 11).

items.statement: In durable self-governed commons, the first sanction for a rule violation is usually small.
items.folk_theory: Deterrence needs big penalties: make cheating unprofitable from the first offence.
items.explanation: Across Ostrom's long-enduring cases first-offence sanctions are graduated and small. Compliance is quasi-voluntary and contingent on believing that others comply and that violations are likely to be seen, so the first sanction's job is to signal that the rule is alive, to the violator and to everyone watching. Harsh first sanctions drive violations and reports underground and erode the information flow monitoring depends on; escalation is held for repeat offenders (Ostrom ch 3, principle 5; ledger rule 30).

items.statement: A commons whose rules satisfy each of Ostrom's eight design principles can be expected to hold.
items.folk_theory: The principles are a recipe: adopt all eight and the commons will hold.
items.explanation: The principles specify no rules; Törbel, the Japanese villages, Valencia and the Philippine zanjeras run different rules under the same structural conditions. They are conditions found in durable cases, not a recipe: a review of 91 empirical studies (Cox, Arnold and Villamayor-Tomás 2010, verified) found them well supported and split three of them, while warning of publication bias and that they capture structure, not processes such as trust and legitimacy. Association in selected cases does not license a guarantee. Use them as a diagnostic checklist, and flag scope for digital or knowledge commons (Ostrom ch 3 and evidence section; ledger C47, rule 29).

items.statement: In a population where everyone learns by copying others, average performance is higher than in a population where everyone learns by trial and error.
items.folk_theory: Copying is a free lunch: a group that copies well outperforms a group that experiments.
items.explanation: Copying pays for the individual: in the social-learning tournament (104 entries, Rendell et al. 2010, verified) copying won even when observing cost no less than innovating, because demonstrators perform their best-known action, so what an observer sees is a sample already filtered toward high payoffs. But the benefit is parasitic on innovators. A population of pure copiers sits on a stale pool and does no better than a population of trial-and-error learners (Rogers's paradox); in the tournament, populations with very high copying rates had lower average fitness. Someone must be paid to innovate, and the winner discounted stale information. The tournament was a simulation, not people (Laland ch 3; ledger rule 39).

items.statement: To tip a group into a new practice, the scarce resource is a small number of members with wide influence.
items.folk_theory: Influencers cause tipping: find the few with wide influence and the rest follow.
items.explanation: Schelling's tipping point is an unstable equilibrium in a threshold distribution or adoption curve: below it participation decays, above it snowballs. Whether a cascade can start depends on whether there are enough low-threshold actors and no gap at the low end, so the scarce resource is people who will act when few others have, not charismatic ones. The influencer framing inverts the model (Schelling ch 3; Easley and Kleinberg ch 17; ledger C30, rule 18).
